issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal when the trial court’s reasons are not reasonable or plausible and its findings cannot reasonably be supported by the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after rejecting the injured eyewitnesses and finding the first report delayed and ante-timed.
The appellate court reassessed the evidence and concluded that the eyewitness accounts were supported by the medical evidence and that the delay had been explained.
The Supreme Court found the trial court’s reasons unreasonable and contrary to the weight of the evidence, and considered the appellate court’s view the only possible view.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court was justified in reversing the acquittal, and the Supreme Court upheld the resulting convictions.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 378 and 379 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, an appellate court’s power to reassess evidence in an appeal against acquittal is extensive. As a matter of prudence, it should give due weight to the trial court’s assessment, the presumption of innocence, the benefit of doubt, and the trial judge’s opportunity to observe witnesses. An acquittal should not be disturbed where its principal grounds are reasonable and plausible; it may be reversed where those grounds are displaced or the findings are manifestly unreasonable or perverse. No earlier case is cited.

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.trial_reasons_conflicted_with_record: The trial court rejected the prosecution case on reasons that conflicted with the evidence and circumstances in the record.
predicates.appellate_evidence_supported_guilt: The appellate court reassessed the record and found evidence supporting the accused’s guilt.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, the trial court’s reasons conflict with the record, and the appellate evidence supports guilt, reversal of the acquittal is justified.

issues.legal_issue: A delay in lodging a first information report does not make it unreliable when the circumstances reasonably explain why the complainant could not report sooner.
material_facts: The occurrence took place at night in winter, outside the village, and the police station was about 18 kilometres away.
The complainant was injured, one of her minor children was also injured, and she took shelter overnight after two people had been killed.
She travelled to hospital the next morning and made her statement there; the police recorded the report on its basis.
The Supreme Court accepted these circumstances as explaining the delay and rejected the claim that the report was ante-timed.
issues.conclusion: The delay in lodging the report was adequately explained and did not justify treating it as ante-timed or unreliable.
issues.legal_principle: The effect of delay in lodging a first information report depends on the circumstances explaining it. The court must assess those circumstances realistically rather than apply a hyper-technical approach. No earlier case is cited.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the prosecution of an alleged criminal offence.
predicates.complainant_was_injured_and_sheltered_ov: The complainant was injured and spent the night sheltering after the occurrence.
predicates.prompt_reporting_was_impracticable: Distance, danger, lack of assistance, or similar circumstances made it impracticable for the complainant to report sooner.
predicates.report_was_made_when_reporting_became_pr: The complainant reported the occurrence when circumstances allowed her to reach assistance.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, when an injured complainant had to shelter overnight, prompt reporting was impracticable, and a report was made when practicable, the delay does not make the report unreliable.

issues.legal_issue: A delay in delivering a special report to a magistrate does not undermine the prosecution when the delay is explained and causes no demonstrated prejudice.
material_facts: The special report reached the magistrate during the night after the constable first delivered it to the Superintendent of Police and then travelled to the magistrate’s residence because the courthouse was locked.
The constable explained that he had waited for the Superintendent of Police to become available and had to locate the duty magistrate.
The statement underlying the report had already been recorded, police had visited the scene, and the inquest reports and seizures had been made.
The appellant identified no prejudice caused by the timing of delivery.
issues.conclusion: The delivery of the special report was not unduly delayed; in any event, the explained delay caused no demonstrated prejudice and did not cast doubt on the report.
issues.legal_principle: Section 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the prescribed report to be sent to the magistrate. Whether delay in doing so undermines the prosecution must be assessed in context, including the explanation for delay and whether it caused prejudice. No earlier case is cited.

rule.if: criminal_case and special_report_delivery_was_delayed and delivery_delay_was_explained and no_prejudice_was_shown

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerns the prosecution of an alleged criminal offence.
predicates.special_report_delivery_was_delayed: The report of the occurrence was delivered to the magistrate later than the time at which it could have been sent.
predicates.delivery_delay_was_explained: The person responsible for delivery gave a circumstantial explanation for the time taken to deliver the report.
predicates.no_prejudice_was_shown: The accused did not demonstrate that the timing of delivery caused prejudice.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, an explained delay in delivering the report to the magistrate does not undermine the prosecution when no prejudice is shown.

issues.legal_issue: Injured eyewitness testimony may be accepted as reliable when the witnesses’ presence is established and their accounts are consistent with one another and with the medical evidence.
material_facts: The complainant and her child both sustained firearm injuries in the occurrence, establishing their presence there.
They gave consistent accounts of the sequence of events and identified the assailants in the tractor’s light.
The medical evidence corroborated the described injuries and, for one deceased person, the account that the shot was fired at close range.

The trial court rejected their testimony on grounds including the absence of immediate reports to village residents, but the Supreme Court found those grounds trivial in light of the night-time circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The injured eyewitnesses were credible, and their testimony supported the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: The presence of witnesses injured in the same occurrence may be accepted as established; their testimony must be assessed with the surrounding evidence, including medical corroboration. The court found the witnesses’ accounts consistent and rejected the proposed contradictions and identification objections on the facts. No earlier case is cited.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction based on eyewitness evidence.
predicates.eyewitnesses_were_injured_in_the_occurre: The eyewitnesses sustained injuries during the occurrence they described.
predicates.eyewitness_accounts_were_consistent: The eyewitnesses gave accounts that agreed on the material events.
predicates.medical_evidence_corroborated_the_accoun: Medical findings supported material features of the eyewitnesses’ accounts.

issues.definition: In a criminal conviction appeal, injured eyewitnesses whose accounts are consistent and medically corroborated provide reliable eyewitness testimony.
